prytaneion.title: Prytaneion
prytaneion.imageAlt: The ruins of the Prytaneion at Ephesus
prytaneion.description: North of the State Agora stands the Prytaneion, an important place in the civic and religious life of Ephesus. It contained the city's sacred hearth. Priests known as the Curetes tended its fire, and their names were inscribed on the building's columns. Statues of Artemis of Ephesus found here during excavations are now displayed in the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk. The re-erected columns help us imagine the building's former appearance.

devlet-agorasi.title: State Agora
devlet-agorasi.imageAlt: View over the State Agora towards the Odeon
devlet-agorasi.description: Also known as the Upper Agora, this area was one of the centres of public life in Ephesus. Unlike the Commercial Agora, it was associated with official and civic gatherings. The square was laid out over an older burial ground. The covered, colonnaded galleries around it were called stoas. The Basilica Stoa to the north and the nearby public buildings reveal its importance in the city's civic life.

basilica-stoa.title: Basilica Stoa
basilica-stoa.imageAlt: Ruins of the Basilica Stoa at Ephesus
basilica-stoa.description: This great colonnaded building ran along the northern side of the State Agora, framing the city's public space. In the year eleven CE, Gaius Sextilius Pollio and his family dedicated it to Artemis, the emperors and the city. Bull heads carved into the Ionic column capitals were among its striking details. The long hall offered shelter from rain and sun and was also associated with public affairs and meetings.

celsus-kutuphanesi.title: Library of Celsus
celsus-kutuphanesi.imageAlt: The façade of the Library of Celsus
celsus-kutuphanesi.description: The Library of Celsus is one of the best-known monuments of Ephesus. In the second century CE, Aquila had it built in memory of his father, the senator Celsus. It was more than a library: the burial chamber of Celsus lay beneath it. Inside were niches and shelves for manuscript scrolls. The two-storey façade visible today was re-erected in the twentieth century using excavated fragments and additional materials. Four statues on the façade represent wisdom, virtue, knowledge and intelligence; the original statues are now in Vienna.

buyuk-tiyatro.title: Great Theatre
buyuk-tiyatro.imageAlt: The Great Theatre of Ephesus and its seating tiers
buyuk-tiyatro.description: The Great Theatre of Ephesus is a monumental open-air structure set into the slope of Panayır Mountain. Its origins reach back to the Hellenistic period, and it was enlarged to its great size under Roman rule. The seating tiers and remains of the stage building convey the scale of this place where communities gathered. Sources give different estimates for its capacity, so an exact figure is difficult to establish. Across from the theatre, Harbour Street once led towards the ancient harbour. Today the remains help us understand the many layers of Ephesian history.

hadrian-tapinagi.title: Temple of Hadrian
hadrian-tapinagi.imageAlt: The façade of the building known as the Temple of Hadrian
hadrian-tapinagi.description: This elegant building on Curetes Street is commonly known as the Temple of Hadrian. The name does not mean its precise function is beyond debate: researchers have studied its role in the imperial cult and its relationship to the baths behind it. Its arch, columns and plant motifs draw attention. Dating to the second century, the façade was re-erected in the twentieth century using excavated fragments. The originals of the reliefs displayed at the front are preserved in the Ephesus Museum; copies are shown here. This small monument offers rich details for understanding the architecture of Ephesus.

trajan-cesmesi.title: Fountain of Trajan
trajan-cesmesi.imageAlt: Ruins of the Fountain of Trajan at Ephesus
trajan-cesmesi.description: The Fountain of Trajan stood on Curetes Street as a monumental display of the city's water supply. An inscription records that the fountain was dedicated to Artemis and Emperor Trajan by the benefactor Tiberius Claudius Aristion and his wife. The basin was framed by an ornate, two-storey façade. A colossal statue of the emperor once stood above the water. Today surviving architectural fragments help us imagine how water, sculpture and civic generosity came together in the public life of Ephesus.

yamac-evler.title: Terrace Houses
yamac-evler.imageAlt: Interior remains of the Terrace Houses at Ephesus
yamac-evler.description: The Terrace Houses are an important archaeological site for understanding domestic life in Roman Ephesus. The houses were built on terraces along the slope of Bülbül Mountain. In the area known as Terrace House Two, wall paintings, mosaics and marble revetments have survived in homes arranged around courtyards. Water installations and traces of underfloor heating reveal the comforts available in some homes. Excavation and conservation have included reassembling fragmented decoration. A protective roof now helps shelter these fragile remains. Check official information before visiting, as access conditions can change.

odeon.title: Odeon / Bouleuterion
odeon.imageAlt: The Odeon and seating tiers at Ephesus
odeon.description: North of the State Agora, this small theatre-shaped building is known as the Odeon or Bouleuterion. Bouleuterion means a meeting place for the city council. The building may also have hosted performances. Stone seating, an orchestra area and a stage building give it the appearance of a small theatre. Inscriptions connect Vedius Antoninus and his family with the building in the second century, but evidence also points to an earlier council house. It is therefore better to think of these remains as a civic space renewed over time, rather than a building created once and never changed.

ticaret-agorasi.title: Commercial Agora
ticaret-agorasi.description: The Commercial Agora was a marketplace near the ancient harbour of Ephesus. Its almost square plan also gave it the name Tetragonos Agora. The area goes back to the Hellenistic period; expansion under Augustus and later alterations changed its appearance. Behind the colonnaded galleries surrounding the open courtyard were shops and workspaces. Gates connected the market to the city's streets. The nearby Library of Celsus and the Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates help us understand this district within the ancient city. The map marker represents an approximate point, not the boundaries of the entire agora.

mazaeus-mithridates.title: Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates
mazaeus-mithridates.imageAlt: The Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates at Ephesus
mazaeus-mithridates.description: The Gate of Mazaeus and Mithridates stands beside the Library of Celsus, at the southern entrance to the Commercial Agora. Inscriptions on the three-arched monument record that it was commissioned by the freedmen Mazaeus and Mithridates in honour of Augustus and his family. The titles in the inscription help date it to around 4–3 BCE. The gate was associated with the arrangement of the agora in antiquity and was re-erected in the twentieth century. Its inscriptions illuminate the city's social relationships as well as its architecture.

memmius.title: Memmius Monument
memmius.description: The Memmius Monument near Curetes Street is an honorary monument from the Roman period. Sources relate that Gaius Memmius commissioned it in connection with his family, and that the Roman dictator Sulla was his grandfather. Architectural fragments and figurative decoration can be seen among the remains. Reconstructions of its original appearance involve interpretation, so the present arrangement should not be treated as a certain image of the ancient building. The nearby Hydreion is a separate water-related structure. The marker approximately represents the area where the two remains stand close together.

skolastika.title: Baths of Scholastica
skolastika.imageAlt: The remains of the Baths of Scholastica
skolastika.description: The Baths of Scholastica near Curetes Street were a Roman complex used for bathing, relaxation and social gatherings. Sources describe an early Roman foundation and a late antique renovation by a woman named Scholastica. The plan included changing, cold, warm and hot rooms. An underfloor heating system helps us understand how the heated spaces worked. The remains reflect interventions from different periods; the walls visible today were not all built at the same time. The nearby latrine, or communal toilet, was a separate public facility.

meryem-kilisesi.title: Church of Mary
meryem-kilisesi.description: The Church of Mary is a large church complex in the northwestern part of ancient Ephesus. It developed within the remains of an earlier Roman building and offers a glimpse into the city's late antique history. A council met at Ephesus in 431, but scholars debate its exact venue and the different phases of the building. This is not the same place as the House of the Virgin Mary outside the ancient city.

efes-stadyumu.title: Stadium of Ephesus
efes-stadyumu.description: The Stadium of Ephesus stretches across the northern part of the ancient city, near the slopes of Mount Panayır. This elongated space was used for various spectacles and competitions in the Roman period. Remains from different phases of its history can still be seen. The map marker represents the wider stadium area; it does not indicate a visitor entrance or walking route.

artemision.title: Temple of Artemis
artemision.description: The Temple of Artemis was part of a great sanctuary dedicated to Artemis of Ephesus. It was celebrated as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. The remains visible today lie near Selçuk, separate from the main ancient city. The temple was rebuilt in different periods, so its surviving remains should not all be assigned to a single phase.

aziz-yuhanna.title: Basilica of Saint John
aziz-yuhanna.imageAlt: Ruins of the Basilica of Saint John
aziz-yuhanna.description: The Basilica of Saint John stands on Ayasuluk Hill in Selçuk. The remains visible today belong to a large Byzantine church built in the sixth century during the reign of Emperor Justinian. Christian tradition associates the site with the tomb of John the Apostle; this association should be understood as a tradition. The basilica lies in the Ayasuluk component of the Ephesus World Heritage site, separate from the ancient city core.

isa-bey.title: İsa Bey Mosque
isa-bey.description: The İsa Bey Mosque stands on the western slope of Ayasuluk Hill in Selçuk, between the Temple of Artemis and the Basilica of Saint John. It was commissioned for İsa Bey in the fourteenth century, during the Aydınid period. Its spacious courtyard and stonework are among its notable features. It is separate from the ancient city core, and the map marker does not indicate the visitor entrance.

oktagon.title: Octagon
oktagon.description: The Octagon is an eight-sided funerary monument on Curetes Street, near the Hellenistic Heroon. For many years it was associated with Arsinoe, the sister of Cleopatra. However, a scientific study published in 2025 found that the examined remains belonged to a young male and could not be Arsinoe's. This result does not, on its own, explain every phase of the monument's use and burials.

heroon.title: Hellenistic Heroon
heroon.description: The Hellenistic Heroon is a monument near the Octagon, at the lower end of Curetes Street. The word heroon describes a monument associated with a hero cult. The structure is sometimes linked to Androclus, the legendary founder of Ephesus, but this identification is uncertain. The remains and proposed reconstructions help researchers explore the Hellenistic history of the city.

latrina.title: Public Latrine
latrina.description: The latrine at Ephesus was a shared toilet facility in the ancient city. It stands near the bath buildings at the lower end of Curetes Street. Its seating and the channel beneath provide a glimpse of water and waste management in Roman urban life. The remains seen today should be considered alongside changes made to the building over time.

liman-caddesi.title: Harbour Street / Arcadiane
liman-caddesi.description: Harbour Street is a broad avenue running from the Great Theatre towards the ancient harbour. It is also known as the Arcadiane and is associated with renovations in the reign of Emperor Arcadius in late antiquity. Colonnaded walkways and surrounding buildings evoke the impressive urban space encountered by people arriving from the harbour. The map marker represents only one point along this long street.

domitian-meydani.title: Domitian Square
domitian-meydani.description: Domitian Square was a public space in the upper city of Ephesus, near the terrace of an imperial cult temple. The monuments and water structures around it help us understand civic life in different periods of the city's history. The square's modern name is associated with the temple. The map marker represents the wider area, not its boundaries or an entrance.
domitian-meydani.imageAlt: Pollio Fountain and temple area near Domitian Square

yedi-uyuyanlar.title: Cave of the Seven Sleepers
yedi-uyuyanlar.description: The Cave of the Seven Sleepers and its surrounding burial ground lie on the slopes of Mount Panayır, outside the ancient city core of Ephesus. The site contains rock-cut tombs and the remains of a church. It is one of several places associated with the story of young people who awoke after a long sleep. Christian and Islamic traditions tell the story in different ways; the identification of this cave with the legend is not an established historical fact. Check current access separately.

ayasuluk.title: Ayasuluk Hill and Citadel
ayasuluk.description: Ayasuluk Hill in Selçuk brings together traces from different periods of the long history of Ephesus. Evidence of early settlement has been found on the hill; fortifications and the Basilica of Saint John later developed here. The walls of the hilltop fortress were built and repaired in different periods. Ayasuluk is part of the Ephesus World Heritage site, in a location separate from the ancient city core.

lukas.title: The so-called Tomb of Saint Luke
lukas.imageAlt: Remains of the so-called Tomb of Saint Luke
lukas.description: The monument known as the Tomb of Saint Luke is a circular structure near the southern entrance area of Ephesus. Despite its name, its identification as Saint Luke's tomb is not established. According to research by Austrian archaeologist Andreas Pülz, it was originally built as a Roman fountain and adapted for use as a church in the fifth century. Its transformation illustrates how ancient buildings were reused in later periods. The map marker represents the remains, not a visitor entrance.

magnesia-kapisi.title: Magnesian Gate
magnesia-kapisi.description: The Magnesian Gate is one of the ancient city gates southeast of Ephesus. It takes its name from the road leading towards Magnesia. The gate and fortifications changed over different periods, and sources disagree on the date of its first construction. This ancient gate is not the same as the modern visitor entrance. The map marker shows an approximate location of the remains; visitor access should be checked separately.

herakles-kapisi.title: Hercules Gate
herakles-kapisi.description: The Hercules Gate is a monumental passage at the upper end of Curetes Street. It takes its name from the reliefs of Hercules on the two surviving pillars. Sources indicate that the reliefs and the gate's present arrangement may belong to different periods. The narrow passage marked the transition from the upper city onto the street. It should not be confused with the ancient Magnesian Gate or Hadrian's Gate.

dogu-gymnasionu.title: East Gymnasium
dogu-gymnasionu.description: The East Gymnasium is a large complex in eastern Ephesus, near the ancient Magnesian Gate. Gymnasiums were associated with physical training and social life, and this complex also included baths. Its surviving remains and excavations help us understand its different sections. The marker represents the wider area; its entrance and current visiting conditions should be checked separately.

domitian-tapinagi.title: Temple of the Sebastoi
domitian-tapinagi.imageAlt: Remains near the Temple of the Sebastoi terrace
domitian-tapinagi.description: The building known as the Temple of Domitian was a temple associated with the imperial cult at Ephesus. It stood on a raised terrace beside Domitian Square and is also called the Temple of the Sebastoi, or the emperors. Much of its upper structure has disappeared, but remains of the terrace and substructure can still be seen. Interpretations of individual statues and building phases require care.

kuretler-caddesi.title: Curetes Street
kuretler-caddesi.description: Curetes Street was one of the main streets linking the upper city of Ephesus with the area around the library. Colonnaded walkways, fountains and monuments lined its sides. Its modern name comes from the Curetes, a group associated with the city's sacred hearth. The street was part of ceremonial routes as well as daily urban life. The marker shows only one point along the long street.

mermer-cadde.title: Marble Street
mermer-cadde.description: Marble Street is an ancient road running from the area of the Library of Celsus towards the Great Theatre. It follows the eastern side of the Commercial Agora and connects important public spaces of the city. Its name comes from the marble paving. The traces visible today reflect a long period of use and changes over time. The marker represents one point, not the whole street or a walking route.

tiyatro-gymnasionu.title: Theatre Gymnasium
tiyatro-gymnasionu.imageAlt: Remains of the Theatre Gymnasium at Ephesus
tiyatro-gymnasionu.description: Across from the Great Theatre and north of Harbour Street stood the Theatre Gymnasium, a Roman complex combining exercise spaces and baths. Built in the second century, it was distinct from the Vedius Gymnasium north of the stadium. A colonnaded exercise court, known as a palaestra, formed part of the complex. The remains and scattered architectural fragments help us imagine how bathing and physical training shaped public life. Later changes and the unfinished state of excavation make some details uncertain. The map pin represents the broader complex, not an entrance. Check current access before visiting.

yukari-hamam.title: Upper Gymnasium and State Agora Baths
yukari-hamam.imageAlt: State Agora Baths seen from a distance
yukari-hamam.description: At the eastern end of the State Agora, near the Odeon, are the remains of the Upper Gymnasium and baths. Parts of this large Roman complex stood against the slope of Mount Pion. Baths were places not only for washing but also for meeting and social life. The complex has not been fully investigated, so questions about its plan and history remain. Some sources call it the Baths of Varius, a name also associated with the Baths of Scholastica on Curetes Street. These are distinct sites. The map pin represents the complex approximately; it is not an entrance.

serapeion.title: So-called Temple of Serapis
serapeion.description: West of the Commercial Agora stands a large sanctuary commonly known as the Temple of Serapis, or the Serapeion. Built during the Roman period, its temple and surrounding architectural remains reflect the monumental character of ancient Ephesus. Despite the familiar name, it is debated whether the sanctuary was actually dedicated to Serapis. Scholars have interpreted inscriptions and finds in different ways and proposed other functions. That uncertainty matters when we look at the surviving remains. The map pin is an approximate centre of the area, not an entrance or an indication of access.

yamac-ev-2.title: Terrace House 2
yamac-ev-2.description: Terrace House Two is a residential block built on the slope south of Curetes Street. Separate homes were arranged in terraces to follow the steep ground. Rooms around courtyards preserve wall paintings, mosaics and marble revetments. Water installations and traces of underfloor heating in some rooms offer a glimpse of domestic life. As the Austrian Archaeological Institute explains, the paintings and mosaics were left in place and a protective roof was erected over the site. This stop focuses on one part of the broader Terrace Houses already in the tour. The pin marks an approximate centre, not an entrance. Check current visiting conditions before you go.

liman-hamamlari.title: Harbour Baths and Gymnasium
liman-hamamlari.imageAlt: Remains of the Harbour Baths at Ephesus
liman-hamamlari.description: The Harbour Baths and Gymnasium formed a large Roman complex in the old harbour district of Ephesus, north of Harbour Street. Baths were combined with spaces for exercise and education. Its earliest phases belong to the Roman imperial period; the complex was later damaged and repaired at different times. The nearby Halls of Verulanus and their broad court were associated with athletic and public life in this area. Only part of the remains has been excavated. The map pin marks the approximate centre of the wider complex, not a visitor entrance or a safe walking route. Check current access before visiting.

meryem-ana-evi.title: House of the Virgin Mary
meryem-ana-evi.imageAlt: Exterior of the chapel known as the House of the Virgin Mary
meryem-ana-evi.description: The House of the Virgin Mary is a shrine on Bülbül Mountain, outside the core of ancient Ephesus. In Christian tradition, Mary is believed to have spent her final years here; that tradition should not be presented as archaeological proof that she lived at this site. The small chapel and its surroundings are a place of significance for Christian and Muslim visitors today. This is not the same place as the Church of Mary inside the ancient city. It is one of the components of the UNESCO Ephesus World Heritage property. The map pin approximately represents the building, not the visitor entrance. Check transport, admission and current visiting conditions before you go.

agora-tapinagi.title: Temple on the State Agora
agora-tapinagi.imageAlt: Temple site in the State Agora
agora-tapinagi.description: A temple once stood in the centre of the State Agora, adding a religious dimension to this civic space. Some sources call it the Temple of Isis, while others regard its dedication as uncertain. We therefore do not treat that identification as established fact. The remaining foundations help us imagine the ancient square, but the map pin represents the approximate site rather than an entrance or a walking route.

yamac-ev-1.title: Terrace House 1
yamac-ev-1.imageAlt: View of the Terrace Houses, categorized as Terrace House 1
yamac-ev-1.description: Terrace House 1 is one of the two residential blocks on the slope south of Curetes Street. Its terraced rooms and housing units reveal the variety of domestic architecture in Ephesus. It is distinct from Terrace House 2, although both belong to the wider Terrace Houses area. The map pin approximately represents the building area, not a visitor entrance. Please check current access before visiting.

hadrian-kapisi.title: Hadrian’s Gate
hadrian-kapisi.imageAlt: Remains of Hadrian’s Gate at Ephesus
hadrian-kapisi.description: Hadrian’s Gate is a monumental gateway near the Library of Celsus, at the western end of Curetes Street. Also called the New Triodos Gate, it marked a meeting point of streets in the ancient city. Its surviving remains belonged to an elaborate structure that once rose through several storeys. Do not confuse it with the Temple of Hadrian elsewhere on Curetes Street. The map pin shows an approximate location, not an entrance or a safe walking route.

alytarkhos-stoasi.title: Alytarchs’ Stoa
alytarkhos-stoasi.imageAlt: Mosaics on Curetes Street near Alytarchs’ Stoa
alytarkhos-stoasi.description: The so-called Alytarchs’ Stoa was a colonnaded hall on the south side of Curetes Street, in front of the Terrace Houses. Because of the slope it had two levels, with shops and workshops behind it. Surviving mosaics with geometric and plant designs recall the richness of this ancient street. Its name comes from an inscription referring to an official responsible for rules at athletic contests. The map pin represents the approximate centre of the long structure, not an entrance or safe walking route.

ask-evi.title: The so-called House of Pleasure
ask-evi.imageAlt: House remains at left, opposite the Library of Celsus
ask-evi.description: Near the Library of Celsus is a group of remains long called the House of Pleasure or brothel. The archaeological site sign explains that this was a mistaken interpretation, and describes private houses with courtyards and shops opening onto the street. The remains of the building complex help us understand domestic life in Roman Ephesus. This is not the same residential block as Terrace House Two. The map pin represents the wider area approximately, not an entrance or walking route.

tiyatro-cesmesi.title: Hellenistic Fountain by the Theatre
tiyatro-cesmesi.imageAlt: Hellenistic fountain house near the Great Theatre
tiyatro-cesmesi.description: The Hellenistic fountain house near the stage building of the Great Theatre is an example of the water architecture of ancient Ephesus. Ionic columns at its front and carefully worked marble are among its distinctive features. The building was also altered in Roman times. It should not be confused with another Hellenistic fountain near the Terrace Houses. The map pin shows an approximate location. Sources differ on its position, and it is not a field survey.

pollio-domitian-cesmesi.title: Pollio Monument and Fountain of Domitian
pollio-domitian-cesmesi.imageAlt: Pollio Monument and Fountain of Domitian area
pollio-domitian-cesmesi.description: On the eastern side of Domitian Square, the Pollio Monument and the Fountain of Domitian stand next to one another. The honorific tomb of Pollio was later incorporated into the fountain complex. According to the site information, the fountain was built in 92 or 93 CE. Its niche held sculptures showing the encounter between Odysseus and Polyphemus; surviving pieces are preserved in the Ephesus Museum. One map pin approximately represents the two closely adjoining structures, not an entrance or walking route.

laecanius-cesmesi.title: Fountain of Laecanius Bassus
laecanius-cesmesi.imageAlt: Remains of the Fountain of Laecanius Bassus
laecanius-cesmesi.description: At the southwest corner of the State Agora stood a monumental water building known as the Fountain of Laecanius Bassus, or Hydrekdocheion. It was donated by the proconsul Gaius Laecanius Bassus around 80 CE. Ornate façades framed its rectangular pool on three sides, and water flowing from sculptures added movement to the architecture. It is distinct from another fountain along the southern side of the agora. The map pin approximately represents the structure, not an entrance or a route.
